title: The 10-Minute Nightly Kitchen Reset (For People Who Hate Morning Dishes)
description: A 10-minute nightly kitchen reset for ADHD brains: 5 steps in the same order every night, so you wake up to a kitchen that's ready for you.
intro:
There's nothing quite like walking into the kitchen in the morning, half-asleep, and being greeted by last night's pots, a sticky counter and a sink full of dishes. It's like a tiny personal attack before coffee.

The nightly kitchen reset is the fix. It's a short, same-every-night routine that takes about ten minutes. Once it's a habit, you'll wake up to a kitchen that's ready for you instead of against you.

Here's the exact order, plus tricks to make it happen when you're tired.

sections.heading: Why the same order every night
sections.body:
Doing the steps in the same order means you don't have to decide what's next. Decisions drain energy, especially at night. When the order is fixed, your body does it while your brain rests.

After a couple of weeks, you'll find yourself doing it almost on autopilot. That's the goal.

sections.heading: The 5 steps
sections.body:
1. **Clear the counters (2 minutes).** Everything that doesn't live on the counter goes back to its spot. Stuff that belongs in another room goes in one basket.
2. **Dishes (4 minutes).** Load the dishwasher. Anything that can't go in soaks in the sink or gets a quick wash with a soap-dispensing brush.
3. **Start the dishwasher (10 seconds).** If it's even three-quarters full, run it. Flip the clean/dirty magnet.
4. **Wipe (2 minutes).** Counters, stovetop and the table. One cloth, one spray.
5. **Close the kitchen (1 minute).** Trash out if it's full, dish towel hung up, lights off.

That's it. Ten minutes, give or take.

sections.heading: Set a trigger
sections.body:
Attach the reset to something that happens every night anyway:

- Right after dinner, before you sit down
- When the kids go to bed
- When your favorite show's first episode ends

The trigger is what makes it automatic. "After X, I do the kitchen." Pick one and stick with it for two weeks.

sections.heading: Make it fun (or at least bearable)
sections.body:
- Put on the same playlist or podcast every night. Your brain starts associating it with the reset.
- Set a visual timer and race it.
- Call someone on speaker while you clean (body doubling!).
- Have a small reward waiting for when you're done, like tea, a bath or a show.

Ten minutes is short enough that a small reward is plenty of motivation.

sections.heading: The low-energy version
sections.body:
Some nights, ten minutes is impossible. On those nights, do only step 2 and step 3: dishes in, dishwasher on. Two minutes.

That's still a reset. Waking up to an empty sink is worth more than a perfect counter.

sections.heading: Make the tools easy
sections.body:
Keep everything you need for the reset right at the sink: dish soap, a brush, a spray and a cloth in a caddy. If you have to go look for the spray, the reset won't happen.

A clean/dirty dishwasher magnet saves arguments about whether the dishes are clean. A small hook for the dish towel means it gets hung up instead of balled on the counter.

sections.heading: When you skip a night
sections.body: Skipping a night isn't a crisis. In the morning, do the low-energy version before coffee, if you can, or right after. Then pick up the regular reset that evening. No catching up, no double shifts. Only tonight.

finds.name: Clean/dirty dishwasher magnet
finds.why: One flip answers the question nobody in your house can remember the answer to.

finds.name: Soap-dispensing dish brush
finds.why: Soap lives in the handle, so rinsing one mug is one step instead of three.

finds.name: Sink sponge caddy with drain tray
finds.search: kitchen sink sponge holder caddy with drain
finds.why: Sponge, brush and soap get one spot, so the sink edge stops being a soggy junk pile.

outro:
Ten minutes tonight means an easier morning tomorrow. Try it for a week and see how it feels to wake up to a clear sink.
